Rocket Trophies for
‘CanSat’ Winners
by Ed Pretty
Our guild was contacted by Maarten Meerman, a member of
the Santa Cruz Woodturners in California but also a former
member of the GVWG, requesting assistance. Maarten is an
actual rocket scientist, designing satellites and was head
hunted by a firm in the US that specializes in miniaturization,
so he now resides in California. Miniaturization is squarely in
Maarten’s wheelhouse; he used to turn various items in 1/144
scale while a member of the GVWG. Typically, his pieces were
mounted on a penny then photographed through a micro
scope. Maarten champions competitions among younger
rocket enthusiasts in Canada, even while residing in the US. He
typically turns whimsical rockets in an art deco style (in a more
common scale) as awards for the competitions.
Given the current border climate, trans-border shipping has
now become impractical for him to make these models then
ship them into Canada. He asked for our assistance, and we
readily granted his request. The completed awards will be
shipped to a GVWG member in Lethbridge, Andre Laroche,
who is also a member of the Chinook woodturners in Leth
bridge. Andre is tasked with getting the awards to their final
destination. All told, this project spans two countries, three
guilds and two disciplines.
Turning “Rock-It”
Producing these whimsical, art deco rocket forms required
preparing the turning blanks for the fin slots, mounting hole,
“portholes” and nose and engine mounts prior to turning. Con
sistent with Kimberly Winkle’s approach to turned furniture
making—“joinery first”, it’s easier to do all of these operations
on a square blank rather than a round form. Prior to turning,
the slots for the fins were cut on the table saw, the portholes
and mounting holes were drilled on the drill press, and the
nose and engine mount holes (mortises) were drilled on the
lathe. The front mortise fit directly onto the drive center and a
temporary center was created to fit the aft mortise for the live
center. The drive center and “faux” engine made convenient
gauges for the end diameters and the midpoint diameter was
the maximum diameter of the stock, so no measurement other
than the position of the maximum diameter was required in
turning the body.
Even though there was also a “proof of concept” version, the
wood used for the body produced enough for five rockets so
one was the “guinea pig” for each operation. Wood for the fins
was milled to the width of the saw kerf then the fin shapes cut
out, the bottom portion matching the 10” radius of the table
saw blade for attaching to the body. The “nose” and engine
were fitted with a tenon to match the drilled mortices fore and
aft. The body, nose, engine and mounting post were all turned
between centers.
The portholes are turned acrylic rod. Each one was faced flat
then parted off the rod. A wooden chuck adapter was made
to hold the individual pieces in a standard chuck for forming
the curved outer surface of each porthole. Aluminum tape was
applied to the flat back of each piece prior to mounting. The
base for the “guinea pig” was a multi-axis turning using a face
plate and waste block. The base was glued to a waste block
with a paper joint. The waste piece was then attached to a face
plate in ¼” increments to turn each “layer” of the base. Once
complete it was a simple matter to split the paper joint and
clean off the bottom.
Got a project you’d like to see featured in our newsletter?
Send photos to: editor@gvwg.ca

President’s Message
by Don Gamble
Every so often I look around the Guild and think, “How on
earth does all of this happen?” And then I remember—it
happens because we have an incredible group of volunteers
quietly making the magic work behind the scenes.
We’re lucky. We already have a strong group of people who
give their time generously and reliably. They’re the reason
April’s Introduction to Bowl Turning class is happening.
They’re the reason we have multiple online TurnerTalks
lined up, another TechTalk ready to go, and a monthly
meeting where no one is wondering why there aren’t chairs,
a lathe setup, and a presenter.
And like any good turning project, the Guild is shaped not
just by the tools in our hands but by the people who step
up at just the right moment. Volunteers come and go, life
shifts, and sometimes folks simply need a break from being
the one who knows where the extension cords live. So every
now and then we look around and say, “Alright, who’s up
next?” We’re also formalizing a few roles so that important
things don’t happen by chance or by whoever wandered
through the door first with a helpful expression.
So this month, I’m putting out a gentle call for a few more
hands. Nothing heavy, nothing dramatic, just an invitation
to help shape the Guild the same way we shape wood, with
care, intention, and a bit of joy in the process.
Here are the roles we’re hoping to fill:
•
Class Turning Coordinator
The person who helps ensure new turners get the criti
cal skills they need for safe, enjoyable turning.
•
Meeting Coordinator
The quiet hero who makes sure meeting setup and
takedown don’t just magically happen.
•
New Member Liaison
The friendly guide who makes sure no first time visitor
is left standing alone, and who helps them meet people,
feel included, and get connected right from the start.
•
Visiting Demonstrator Team Member
A relaxed, collaborative role for anyone who enjoys
talking to people and helping bring interesting turners
to our Guild. You might help reach out to potential dem
onstrators, chat with them about what they teach, gath
er a few details for the website, or help the team sort
out dates. Nothing heavy, nothing solo, and no need
to be an expert. You’re simply part of the small group
that helps keep our Visiting Demonstrator program fun,
varied, and running smoothly.
•
Sawdust Huddles Leader
And this one is a little different. Sawdust Huddles are
something we’re just getting started. Think small, infor
mal meetups like coffee chats, shop tours, or come see
this odd jig I made gatherings. We don’t need a super
hero here, just someone who enjoys people and wants
to help spark a bit more connection between meetings.
And since this month’s President’s Challenge is The Space
Between, it’s worth saying that what fills the space between
our meetings, our classes, and our demos is exactly this,
people stepping forward, helping out, and keeping the Guild
alive with energy and goodwill. That’s the real grain running
through everything we do.
Now for the part where I encourage a tiny bit of bravery.
If you know someone who would be perfect for one of
these roles, give them a nudge. And if that someone might
actually be you, have a quiet conversation with yourself. You
might discover you’ve been missing out on one of the most
rewarding parts of Guild life.
If you benefit from the classes, the talks, the demos, the
meetings, or simply the sense of community, consider get
ting involved. It doesn’t have to be a big commitment. It just
has to be you, offering a bit of what you can.
If any of these roles spark your interest or even just your
curiosity, come talk to me or any Board member. We’d love
to chat.
See you at the next meeting.

Editor’s Notes
by Britchie
Hello everyone.
As the new Editor, I’m excited to deliver to you the next gen
eration of our newsletter. I’ve taken over the role from Steve
Fairbairn who has worked behind the scenes to publish this
on a monthly basis for the past 5+ years. On behalf of us all, I
would like to thank Steve for his dedication and trust that he
was not trying to create some kind of precedent..! :-)
As you look through this month’s issue, a few things will be
immediately apparent. Firstly, I’ve given the newsletter a
name: The Circular. I tried to come up with something that
would work for us within the two main disciplines of our
craft—spindle and bowl turning. And it’s also a riff on getting
Guild events and news out to you.
What should also stand out to you is the new look and feel.
I’ve run with a clean and modern aesthetic, focusing on
legibility and flexibility within the same familiar framework.
The new colours and style are the start of a brand which will
evolve and mature as time goes on. And I want to feature
more of the people that make our Guild a success (I’m three
years in and still don’t know who many of you are!).
My vision for our newsletter goes beyond these graphic
details. I see it as a vehicle that can help us drive more
engagement and increase our profile within the AAW and
wider community. To that end, I’m drafting a set of content
guidelines that will help to shape the newsletter in support
of these goals. I already have some ideas for some new seg
ments but I’m also interested in any that you have, and how
you can get involved. So let’s talk about that.
..........
In this issue we have several in-depth articles starting with
Ed Pretty’s detailed description of his ‘Rock-It’ trophy
genesis, how-to notes from Allan Cusworth’s Guild meeting
demonstration and an article on using new technology by
Don Gamble. We also have what I think is an impressive
showcase of member work in the Instant Gallery and Presi
dent’s Challenge Gallery this month. Kudos to you all.
Enjoy reading!

E D I T O R S ’ S N O T E S
15% Discount for GVWG Members
If you give the cashier your phone number, you will only get
the store 5% non-Guild discount. By saying GVWG instead you
get the 15% Guild discount.
If you are buying something that needs a warranty, just give
them your Name and Address and that will go on the electron
ic file. If the item you are buying has a flyer sale that is better
than the 15%, then you will automatically get the better rate.
Every purchase you make in the store by using this process
adds to our GVWG Credit account which we use to buy KMS
gift certificate prizes. We even bought our Laguna lathe for
Sapperton Hall with this! By doing this you are giving yourself
a better discount and helping the guild at the same time.
If you are an out-of-town Guild member, all you have to do is
type in GVWG as the customer name when buying, and type in
your full name, address etc. in the ‘ship-to’ field and you will
get the 15% discount.
The 15% is an average savings and is based on the cost mar
gins from that manufacturer. This does not apply to published
special flyer items. If we all do this, we can even get up to a
bigger discount level in future!

Inside/Outside
Ornamental Bud Vase
by Allan Cusworth
How to make an Inside/Outside Vase
Plan
•
Draw a sketch with dimensions. This finished vase will
be 3½” diameter x 7¼” high.
Blank Preparation
•
Cut 4 blanks 1½” x 1½” by exactly 9” long making sure
that the angles are exactly 90° square. (These can be cut
from one 9” long square block if wood grain orientation
is important.)
•
Assemble the blanks together so the desired outside
surfaces are on the outside.
•
Mark the outside corners at the top end on each blank
with T1, T2, T3, & T4 clockwise. The “T” indicates the
top of ornament. Draw an arrow pointing towards the
center on each blank. You may decide not to add the
arrows after you have made a few pieces.
(Continues on the next page)

G U I L D M E M B E R D E M O
This month’s GVWG member demonstration
was performed by one of our long standing
members—Allan Cusworth. Allan showed
us how to make an ornamental bud vase
using a quartered composite blank that is
first turned on the inside, and then on the
outside. Here’s Allan’s presentation notes
so you can follow his steps in making your
own version. Happy turning!

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | A P R I L 2 0 2 6
Blank Assembly
•
Rotate each piece 180° so the outside (“T”) corners now
are at the inside center of the blank. I like to wrap a rub
ber band around the assembly to keep the orientation
of the blank intact until the next step.
•
Rotate T1 and T2 pieces ¼ turn counterclockwise &
make a witness mark to indicate the surfaces to be
glued together.
•
Rub the witness marked surfaces on an 80-grit sanding
block to ensure surfaces are flat.
•
Glue those two pieces together with a piece of craft or
newspaper between the glue joint.
•
Do the same with T3 and T4 pieces.
•
Allow about an hour for the glue to set.
•
Rub the flat surface on an 80-grit sanding block to en
sure surfaces are flat.
•
Glue the 2 flat pieces together with a piece of craft or
newspaper between the glue joint.
•
Allow the glued-up blank to cure overnight.
•
Dimple the exact center of each end. Drill a 1/8” diame
ter hole ¼” deep on both ends to reduce the chance of
splitting the blank.
Turning the “Inside”
•
Mount the blank between centers with the bottom end
towards the tailstock.
•
Mark the vase inside shape length dimensions on the
sides of the blank. Use a square to extend the marks
onto at least two sides.
•
Cut out the shape of the inside profile. Do NOT round
off the square corners at the end of the piece.
•
Cut the shape a little less than half way when looking
from the flat side of the assembly.
•
Sand the “inside” surface to finish grit. Do not over
sand. Maintain the sharpness of the bottom inside
corners. Finish the “inside” surface. Use a friction polish
if you want to process right away. You can paint it.
•
Separate the pieces using a flat chisel and rotate the
pieces 180°. There’s no need to remove the paper.
Reassembling the Blank for Turning the “Outside”
•
Rotate each section 180° (2 flips) so the outside “T”
corners are back on the outside.
•
Rotate sections T1 & T2 over ¼ turn counterclockwise
and make a witness mark on the surfaces of sections to
be glued together.
•
Rub those witness marked surfaces on flat 80-grit sand
ing block to ensure the surfaces are flat.
•
Flip them back over ¼ turn and glue sections T1 & T2
with the T#’s on the outside corners.
•
Make sure the inside bottom edge surfaces are even.
•
Do the same with T3 & T4 sections.
•
This makes two flat sections (T1 & T2) and (T3 & T4).
•
Sand the two flat glue surfaces on an 80-grit sanding
block and glue them together.
•
Make sure the inside bottom edge surfaces are even.
•
Make sure the 1/8” diameter ¼” deep holes at exact
center of each end are still there.
Turning the Outside
•
Mount the reassembled blank between centers with the
bottom end towards the tailstock.
•
Round off the tailstock end and make a tenon to fit 2”
chuck jaws.
•
Remount the blank in a chuck while lining it up with a

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | A P R I L 2 0 2 6
point in the live center.
•
Start to round off the blank leaving the slats area
strong.
•
Shape the top area at the tailstock end to establish the
top surface of the vase.
•
Dimple the exact center of the top and drill the open
ing hole with a Forstner bit. The size is determined by
the end use.
•
If adding a glass tube, the bit size required is the OD of
the tube. To get a slip fit use a dowel with a slot in the
end and insert a piece of 80 grit sandpaper to slightly
increase the hole diameter.
•
Flare out the opening to create the top surface of the
vase.
•
Place a cone on the live center, bring it up to the hole
and continue shaping the vase to its final shape.
•
Sand the outside surfaces to finish grit.
•
Add any decorative burn rings as desired.
Finishing the Vase
•
Finish with two three coats of wipe-on polyurethane.
•
Don’t get any finish on the inside of the hole.
•
Part off the vase. Reverse onto a friction chuck to com
plete the bottom of the base.
•
Add desired decorations to the bottom of the base
(rings) and sign it. Finish the base.

G U I L D M E M B E R D E M O
About Allan Cusworth
Allan started wood turning at school in Ontar
io and has been a GVWG member since 2000.
He creates goblets with captive rings and
is also recognized for his bowls, platters and
unique vessels, making each creation unique by
embellishing the wood’s natural grain patterns and colouration.

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | A P R I L 2 0 2 6
YOUR PERSONAL SAFETY
Always wear Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) such as
approved safety glasses or goggles that include side protec
tors. Use a full face shield for larger bowl, vessel, or any turning
involving chucks and faceplates. Wear a dust mask or an air
filtration helmet in conjunction with proper ventilation and/or
a dust collection system as appropriate. Remember—it’s the
fine airbourne particles that are harmful to your respiratory
system. Wear hearing protection during extended periods of
turning.
Tie back long hair and avoid long sleeves or loose clothing.
Remove rings and other jewelry, or any dangling objects that
may catch on rotating parts or accessories.
Stay alert. Watch what you are doing. Pay close attention to
unusual sounds or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the
cause. Don’t operate machines when you are tired or under
the influence of drugs or alcohol.
WORKING SAFELY WITH YOUR LATHE
Ensure your workpiece is securely fastened. When using a
faceplate, be certain the workpiece is solidly mounted with
stout screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws as a minimum).
Do not use drywall or deck screws. When turning between
centres, check the workpiece is firmly mounted between the
headstock and tailstock and rotate your workpiece forwards/
backwards by hand to make sure it clears the toolrest and bed
before turning the lathe on.
Check all locking devices on the tailstock and tool rest as
sembly (rest and base) are tight before operating the lathe.
Check the speed of your lathe BEFORE turning it on. Use
slower speeds for larger diameters or rough pieces and higher
speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced.
Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is
balanced. If the lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the speed.
If the workpiece vibrates, always stop the machine to under
stand why. As a starting point, consult your operator’s manual
for recommended speeds for a particular lathe. Ensure the
lathe speed is compatible with the diameter of the blank.
Stay clear of danger zones directly behind and in front of the
workpiece. They are the most likely areas for a piece to travel
as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of
this zone when turning on the lathe, keeping your hand on the
switch in case you need to turn the machine off. When observ
ing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
Turn the lathe off before adjusting anything including the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
Always remove chuck keys, adjusting wrenches, and knock
out bars immediately after use. Never leave them in place,
even for a moment. Always remove the tool rest before sand
ing, finishing, or polishing operations.
Know your capabilities and limitations. An experienced
woodturner is capable of lathe speeds, techniques, and proce
dures not recommended for beginning turners.
Exercise extra caution when using stock with cracks, splits,
checks, bark pockets, knots, irregular shapes or protuberanc
es. Beginners should avoid these types of stock until they have
greater knowledge of working such wood.
Hold turning tools securely on the toolrest, holding the tool
in a controlled but comfortable manner. Always contact the
tool rest with the tool before contacting the wood.
Never work with a lathe in reverse unless the chuck is using
a locking set-screw. It is possible for a chuck or faceplate to
unscrew unless it is fitted securely on the lathe spindle.
Don’t overreach. Keep proper footing and keep your balance

S A F E T Y G U I D E L I N E S
(Continues on the next page)
You mostly work on your own so safety is
YOUR responsibility. Please take the time to
read our safety guidelines and make them part
of your daily turning practice. Be safe out there!

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | A P R I L 2 0 2 6
at all times.
Keep tools sharp and clean for better and safer performance.
Don’t force a dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose for which
it was not designed or intended.
Consider your work environment. Don’t use a lathe in damp
or wet locations. Do not use in presence of flammable liquids
or gases, and always keep a fully-charged fire extinguisher
close at hand. Keep your work area well lit.
Guard against electric shock. Inspect electric cords for dam
age. Avoid the use of extension cords.
Never leave a lathe running unattended. Turn power off.
Don’t leave lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
SAFETY MAINTENANCE
Keep your lathe in good repair. Ensure belt guards or protec
tive covers are in place. Check for damaged parts, alignment,
binding of moving parts, and other conditions that may affect
its operation.
Read and follow safety guidelines for your lathe and other
workshop equipment. Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially bandsaws and chainsaws.

V I S I T I N G P R E S E N T E R
Mastering the Art of Precision:
A Live Woodturning
Experience
with Matt Monaco
Matt Monaco is a highly respected woodturner, educator, and
craftsman, known for his expert precision, refined tool tech
niques, and mastery of classical design. With over 20 years of
experience, Matt runs a full-time woodturning studio in the
Ozark region of Missouri, where he creates signature series
bowls, lidded containers, and spindle-turned pieces for craft
enthusiasts, interior designers, and fine furniture makers.
His journey in woodturning began through apprenticeship
and professional training, making him one of the few tradi
tional woodturners preserving classic techniques today. His
approach focuses
on precision
sharpening,
refined cutting
methods, and an
intuitive under
standing of form,
allowing him to
create pieces that
are both tactile
and visually striking. Matt spent time at Shackleton Thomas
Furniture & Pottery, honing his ability to craft finely detailed
work for high-end furniture production.
Beyond his studio, Matt is a Fine Woodworking Contributor
& Ambassador, sharing his expertise through articles, work
shops, and online courses. His demonstrations highlight bowl
turning, spindle work, and
traditional techniques,
giving attendees insight
into his refined approach
to shaping wood. His
signature pieces, such as
Southwestern-inspired
bowls and turned serving
dishes, combine historical
influences with modern
craftsmanship.
Committed to education, Matt teaches at the Port Townsend
School of Woodworking, guiding students through lathe
work, tool handling, and design principles. His upcoming
live demonstration offers a rare chance to see his techniques
firsthand, providing insights into precision turning, form refine
ment, and the artistry behind functional wooden objects.
Don’t miss Matt
Monaco’s live demon
stration—a unique
opportunity to learn
from his expertise
and elevate your own
woodworking skills.
Whether you’re a sea
soned turner or new
to the craft, Matt’s en
gaging style and tech
nical mastery make
this event a must-attend for all woodworking enthusiasts!
For more details on his work, visit his website.

The Vessel of
Hephaestus
Fire, Carbon, and a New
Way of Learning
by Don Gamble
At the start of this project, I was no expert in surface tech
niques. My skills in carving and pyrography were modest,
and painting was an entirely new challenge. What I had was a
hollow form turned from Cherry, a hazy vision of the finished
piece, and a deep curiosity paired with a readiness to learn.
Drawing on my woodworking skills, I carved the initial forms—
lava flows, tiles, and fissures. In my mind, the lava flows
embodied the vessel being superheated, while the tiles and
fissures symbolized the vessel being torn apart by the pains
and failures of mankind. Using my limited pyrography skills, I
deepened the fissure walls and gave the lava flows a rugged,
flowing texture.
Painting presented my steepest learning curve. Translating the
ideas in my mind into purposeful color application was daunt
ing. I struggled to clearly articulate my vision, even to myself,
making it difficult to imagine the finished piece. Though I had
books, online resources, and occasional advice from skilled
artists, I lacked steady, detailed mentorship to help build a
strong vision and develop my painting skills. To bridge this
gap, I turned to an unexpected partner: Microsoft’s AI chat tool,
Copilot.
I shared my vision with the AI: “It is a piece where the pains
of mankind are reduced to carbon and reborn through the
intense heat of an unseen force.” Through a series of chats, this

concept evolved into a Greek myth—The Vessel of Hephaes
tus, which shaped all texturing and coloring decisions going
forward. The full myth—crafted through our early exchanges
serving as the vessel’s guiding legend (see sidebar).
My conversations with Copilot ranged from clarifying basic
terminology to in-depth discussions lasting hours. I shared my
thoughts and next steps while seeking critique and guidance.
I asked for advice on selecting paints, mixing ratios, brushes,
and techniques. These ongoing dialogues resembled those
with a thoughtful mentor—not one who directs the way, but
one who listens, responds, and requires you to be inquisitive
and self-starting. With each exchange, my confidence grew,
and my collection of paints, mediums, glazes, and brushes
expanded from a few essentials to several boxes, each new
tool marking progress on my journey. The AI, accessible as an
app on my phone, even guided me in real-time through the
overwhelming array of products at the art store—a place that
initially felt foreign and intimidating.
Our exchanges were both poetic and practical. At one point, I
asked how to revive the yellow seam in the center of the lava
flows that had dulled under layers of soot applied through
speckling and glaze. The AI replied: “Think of the seam as the
spine of heat in your flow. Re-establish it with Hansa Yellow
Light, then glaze lightly with Burnt Orange to integrate it. The
goal isn’t to repaint but to let the yellow breathe again—a fila
ment of light inside the fracture.” At other times, the guidance
was straightforward: “To suggest minerals within the carbon
deposits, add a touch of Cerulean Blue (Chromium) to the
Payne Grey and Carbon Black mixture.”

The Legend of Hephaestus’s Vessel
In the hidden forge where sparks fall like stars,
Hephaestus gathers the burdens of human
kind—grief, failure, longing, and striving. He
does not cast them aside, but lowers them into
a hollow vessel of obsidian, a crucible of fire and
will. Within the breath of the bellows, mortal
troubles ignite. They blacken, fracture, and col
lapse into carbon. Yet from the cracks emerges
radiance, from ruin, molten seams of light.
For Hephaestus, carbon is never an ending but
a beginning. From ash, he calls forth flame.
From fracture, he summons form. From sorrow,
he shapes vessels strong enough to carry hope.
From carbon itself, he forges rebirth. Thus, the
Vessel of Hephaestus endures—not as wood or
fire alone, but as a reminder that even in our
deepest fissures, light and renewal wait to be
revealed.

The AI’s guidance never replaced my judgment. For example,
I chose not to follow the recommendation to glaze Burnt
Orange but instead used Pyrrole Orange to lift the seam back
into view with a stronger orange halo. This decision came after
detailed discussion about how different orange glazes would
impact the appearance of the lava seam. The AI provided
language and an educated sounding board to understand
why certain techniques worked and how to recover when they
didn’t.
I learned how base coats establish depth, how heavy-body
paints behave differently from fluid ones, how glazes and me
diums control sheen, and how layering colors changes the way
light reflects back to the eye.
As the piece grew more complex, with more layers of color
and texture, I reached a point where words could no longer
capture what I saw or felt. The AI had never been a steady
guide, but rather a sounding board—helping me discover my
course without charting it for me. When that sounding board
could no longer keep pace, I felt disarmed at first. Yet this was
the turning point: I had to trust my own instincts—like a cook
tasting and seasoning without a recipe, until the vessel itself
told me it was complete.
The finished vessel stands as both object and experiment.
It is a hollow wooden form, dressed in the language of fire,
carrying the story of Hephaestus and the lessons of a new way
of learning. For me, it is proof that even in a craft as ancient
as ours, there are always new stories to tell, new tools to learn
from, and new fires to kindle—some sparked by gods, others
by curiosity.

About Don Gamble
After a career in IT, Don channels the
same problem solving mindset into
woodturning and exploring new artistic
directions. He began turning in 2019 and
has studied with many great woodturners,
carrying a bit of each influence into his bowls, platters,
and hollow forms. As our Guild President, Don fosters a
learning, collaborative and welcoming community for
turners of all skill levels.
